lab_title: The Retrograde Puzzle: Why Mars Loops Backward in the Night Sky
top_level_objectives: Describe the observed pattern of apparent retrograde motion, in which Mars slows, reverses into a westward loop, and then resumes eastward drift against the background stars
Explain why the geocentric model required epicycles to account for retrograde loops and why this became a central problem for that model
Demonstrate how retrograde motion emerges naturally from the heliocentric model as the faster inner Earth overtakes the slower outer Mars
Compare the retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and relate the differences to each planet's distance from the Sun

scenes.brief_purpose: Ground students in the raw observation of retrograde motion as ancient sky-watchers experienced it, establishing the phenomenon that the rest of the lab explains.
key_visuals: A night-sky dome overhead showing familiar zodiac constellations as a fixed backdrop
A bright reddish dot labeled Mars positioned among the stars
A calendar or date counter advancing week by week
A faint trail marking Mars's past positions against the stars
student_actions: Look up at the AR night sky and locate the labeled point of light identified as Mars
Advance time week by week and watch Mars drift slowly eastward relative to the constellations
Continue advancing time until Mars visibly slows, stops, and reverses into a westward loop
Note the dates at which Mars begins and ends its backward motion

scenes.brief_purpose: Help students recognize retrograde motion as a defined pattern with a characteristic looping shape rather than a random wobble.
key_visuals: The persistent glowing trail of Mars's path forming an S-curve or loop against the star field
Labeled markers indicating the start of retrograde, the reversal point, and the return to normal motion
A small inset timeline showing the roughly two-month duration of the loop
student_actions: Replay the full motion sequence and observe the complete loop traced by Mars
Place markers on the sky where Mars appears to pause before and after the backward segment
Estimate how long the westward loop lasts compared to the normal eastward drift
Summarize in their own words the pattern they have observed

scenes.brief_purpose: Show how ancient astronomers preserved an Earth-centered universe by inventing epicycles, illustrating why the model grew complicated.
key_visuals: Earth fixed at the center of a set of nested circles
Mars riding on a small circle (epicycle) whose center travels along a larger circle (deferent)
The looping path that the epicycle produces as seen from central Earth
student_actions: Manipulate the epicycle motion and watch how the small-circle-on-big-circle geometry produces a backward loop
Adjust the epicycle until the loop it produces matches the retrograde pattern observed from Earth
Reflect on how many adjustments are needed to fit the observations and why this troubled astronomers

scenes.brief_purpose: Transition students from the Earth-bound perspective to a top-down view of the solar system, revealing both planets on simple circular orbits.
key_visuals: A zoomed-out view of the Sun at the center with Earth and Mars on separate concentric orbits
Earth moving noticeably faster along its inner orbit than Mars on its outer orbit
Smooth, circular orbital paths with no epicycles
Sight-lines drawn from Earth through Mars out to the distant star background
student_actions: Rotate and zoom the solar-system model to view the orbits from above
Run time forward and watch Earth catch up to and overtake Mars
Observe how the Earth-to-Mars sight-line sweeps forward and then backward against the far stars as Earth passes Mars

scenes.brief_purpose: Cement understanding by directly linking the overtaking event in the heliocentric view to the retrograde loop seen from the ground.
key_visuals: A split or picture-in-picture display: heliocentric top-down view on one side, Earth-sky view on the other
The projected position of Mars on the star background updating in sync in both views
A highlighted interval marking exactly when the sight-line reverses and when the sky-view loop occurs
student_actions: Play both views simultaneously and confirm the loop appears in the sky exactly when Earth overtakes Mars
Identify the moment of closest approach and relate it to the middle of the retrograde loop
Explain retrograde motion using the passing-car analogy in their own words

scenes.brief_purpose: Extend the relative-motion principle to other outer planets, showing that distance from the Sun controls how dramatic the loop appears.
key_visuals: The heliocentric model expanded to include Jupiter and Saturn on wider orbits
Side-by-side retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn traced against the stars
A comparison panel showing orbital speeds and loop sizes for each planet
student_actions: Switch the outer planet from Mars to Jupiter to Saturn and observe each retrograde loop
Compare the size and duration of the loops among the three planets
Predict and then verify that the more distant planet produces the smaller, less dramatic loop
Articulate why greater distance from the Sun weakens the relative-motion effect
